findings.headline: Of £23m savings targeted for 2026/27, £0.6m is projected to fall short and £3.9m (ten initiatives) have delivery concerns; Better Leicestershire Programme's £27m identified savings not yet built into MTFS
findings.detail: Savings delivery is showing early slippage. Four initiatives totalling £0.6m are expected to fall short of 2026/27 target: Customer Programme (£130k), Ways of Working office space (£50k), ASC Lightbulb Service review (£160k), and Defining CFS for the Future Phase 2 (£250k). Additionally, ten initiatives totalling £3.9m are 'tracking with some delivery concerns.' The Better Leicestershire Programme from the Efficiency Review identified £27m of potential savings over the current MTFS period (rising to £60m by 2030/31), but these have not yet been incorporated into the MTFS as only savings with sufficient confidence are being included, and the programme is still being mobilized.
findings.matters: If the council cannot reliably deliver 3% of current-year targets, confidence in much larger projected savings (£27–60m) diminishes. Savings shortfalls lead to larger-than-forecast deficits, faster reserve depletion, and service cuts. This signals execution risk in the council's financial recovery plan.
findings.figures: £23m total 2026/27 savings target; £0.6m falling short (four initiatives); £3.9m with delivery concerns (ten initiatives); Better Leicestershire identified £27m potential (£60m by 2030/31)
findings.quote: The majority of these savings are on target with four exceptions with a total value of £0.6m which is reflected in the budget monitoring position that are expected to fall short of target in the current financial year.

findings.headline: Two new unitary authorities to take effect from 1 April 2028, with financial impact 'still to be determined' and no detailed impacts yet included in MTFS, but transition costs held in reserves
findings.detail: The government has announced that Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland will be reorganised into two new unitary authorities from 1 April 2028. The council acknowledges that 'a significant amount of work will now be required to determine the financial impact on the new authorities and this will evolve over the coming months.' Funding towards estimated transition costs is included in reserves, but detailed financial impacts of the reorganisation have not yet been incorporated into the MTFS.
findings.matters: Local government reorganisation is high-cost and high-risk, with uncertain financial consequences. The council is committing reserves to undefined transition costs before impacts are known. Lenders need clarity on liability allocation (particularly the £79m+ SEND deficit split) and what additional financial pressures might emerge that affect post-2028 financial stability.
findings.figures: 1 April 2028 effective date; two new unitary authorities; transition costs held in reserves but amount not specified
findings.quote: The Government's model for Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland has recently been announced with the establishment of two new unitary authorities for Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland, to take effect on 1 April 2028. A significant amount of work will now be required to determine the financial impact on the new authorities and this will evolve over the coming months.

findings.headline: Adult social care cost pressures emerging across multiple services: supported living up £1.3m, direct payments up £1.2m, Better Care Fund up £1.2m, with service user numbers continuing to rise above demographic trends
findings.detail: Multiple cost drivers are pressuring the adult social care budget. Supported living shows a £1.3m overspend driven by a sharp increase in average hours per service user (+4%) observed in Q4 2025/26 and continuing into 2026/27, plus very high-needs packages above average cost. Direct Cash Payments show a £1.2m overspend (shortfall on clawbacks £0.5m, higher average package costs £0.7m). Better Care Fund income is £1.2m down due to lower activity on discharge-to-assess income (£1.6m forecast vs £2.8m budget). Service user numbers in homecare rose 2.85% between February and May 2026 (2,730 to 2,813), with historic data suggesting further increases expected in autumn as young adults transition from children's services.
findings.matters: Adult social care is one of the largest council budgets with demand-led costs outside council control. Sustained growth in service user numbers, increased hours per user, and escalating average package costs signal structural cost growth that will persist. These are key indicators of sustained financial pressure on council resources.
findings.figures: Supported living £1.3m overspend; Direct Cash Payments £1.2m overspend; Better Care Fund £1.2m overspend; Homecare service users 2,730→2,813 (+2.85%) Feb-May 2026; average hours 10.8 per user
findings.quote: The overspend reflects a sharp increase in the average hours per service user (+4%) that was observed in the final quarter of 2025/26 that is expected to continue into 2026/27. There are also some very high-needs packages that started in the final quarter of 2025/26 that are significantly above the normal average package cost.

findings.headline: Around ten schools likely to require additional funding for expansion, with council unable to fund shortfalls and describing position as 'significant Education and financial risk'
findings.detail: The council has committed discretionary revenue funding to cover school place provision shortfalls: £12.6m in summer 2025 and £6.7m in February 2026. A further ten schools are likely to require additional funding in the new MTFS. Shortfalls are caused by construction cost inflation outpacing developer contribution indexation, new requirements (zero-carbon, sprinkler systems) not anticipated in legacy Section 106 agreements, and cuts to DfE Basic Need capital funding following the DfE's change to funding methodology (which now applies minimum place thresholds and discounts pupils from housing developments). Recent schemes have experienced cost overruns from planning delays and additional conditions.
findings.matters: The council is diverting revenue to cover capital project shortfalls that should be funded from government grant or developer contributions. This diverts resources from core service delivery and signals an inability to fund essential infrastructure from standard sources. Repeated cost escalation and unfunded requirements indicate delivery risk.
findings.figures: £12.6m discretionary funding summer 2025; £6.7m February 2026; around ten additional schools requiring funding in new MTFS
findings.quote: There are around a further ten schools that are likely to require additional funding in the new MTFS. The department is urgently reviewing the position and options to reduce the costs and funding shortfalls. However, this remains a significant Education and financial risk to the Council.

findings.headline: Revenue budget balanced only through use of £10.6m from reserves in 2026/27, following £6m in 2024/25 and £5m in 2025/26, with projected medium-term funding gaps of £34m rising to £85m by 2029/30
findings.detail: The council required £15m from reserves to balance the initial 2026/27 budget (reduced to £10.6m through in-year underspend), perpetuating a three-year pattern of reserve depletion (£6m in 2024/25, £5m in 2025/26). The original MTFS forecast funding gaps of £34m in 2027/28 rising to £85m by 2029/30 despite £115m savings being targeted and £313m already delivered since 2010. The report warns explicitly that 'ongoing reliance on reserves to balance the budget should be avoided' because reserves 'can only be used once' and this approach 'does not solve the structural imbalance between income and expenditure that inflation and spending pressures are causing.'
findings.matters: Systematic depletion of reserves to cover recurring deficits signals the council cannot sustainably fund services from taxation and government grant. This is a key credit indicator—once reserves are exhausted, the council must choose between cutting services, raising tax significantly, or borrowing, all constrained options that affect lender security.
findings.figures: £15m→£10.6m from reserves 2026/27; £6m 2024/25; £5m 2025/26; £115m savings targeted in current MTFS; £313m already delivered since 2010; £34m funding gap 2027/28 rising to £85m by 2029/30
findings.quote: To balance the budget the use of reserves or other short-term measures may need to be considered as was the case with the County Council's 2024/25, 2025/26 and 2026/27 budgets, with £6m, £5m and £15m respectively being required from reserves to balance the initial budgets. Reserves can only be used once and ongoing reliance on reserves to balance the budget should be avoided.

findings.headline: High Needs Block overspend of £62.2m in 2026/27, with cumulative DSG deficit of £79.2m and projected growth to £400m by March 2030 before government support
findings.detail: The council faces a chronic SEND funding crisis. The cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit at end of 2025/26 was £79.2m, driven by sustained growth in funded Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs). Active EHCPs reached 8,786 at January 2026 (193% increase since 2016) and 9,188 by mid-July 2026. The paper states that if demand continues on similar trajectory, the deficit could reach £400m by March 2030. Government support covers only 90% of deficits as at March 2026; no confirmation yet of support for 2026/27 and 2027/28 deficits. The paper explicitly describes this position as 'unsustainable.'
findings.matters: A £79m accumulated liability growing by demand pressures outside the council's control, with only partial government cover confirmed and a potential four-year trajectory to £400m, represents a material unfunded obligation that constrains financial flexibility and credit quality.
findings.figures: £62.2m High Needs overspend 2026/27; £79.2m cumulative DSG deficit at end 2025/26; projected £400m by March 2030; 8,786 active EHCPs at January 2026 (193% increase since 2016); 9,188 EHCPs mid-July 2026 (5% increase in first half calendar year); government support covers 90% of March 2026 deficit only
findings.quote: Despite current planned mitigations, at the levels of expected and/or projected growth, the financial position is unsustainable. As such it is essential that the planned measures to contain ongoing growth are successful, and further mitigations and actions are actively considered to reduce the projected financial burden on the DSG High Needs funding block.

findings.detail: Multiple initiatives centre on generating new income (Lane Rental, asset monetization, investment returns) or on implementing 'innovative' commissioning models described as pilot approaches. Income generation is typically harder to realize and more volatile than service cost reduction.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a budget plan is built on realistic, proven methods or on speculative income schemes. Reliance on multiple unproven income initiatives increases risk that the council fails to achieve its rebalancing targets.

findings.matters: The council is creating permanent specialist staffing capacity that will be needed beyond 2029, but has no confirmed funding source after the grant expires. From April 2029, the service will either need funding from the council's own budget or must be significantly reduced.

This wording indicates the council has historic deficits and that at least 10% will not be covered by the grant. The document does not quantify these deficits or the unfunded portion.

findings.matters: LGR is a major structural change affecting asset management, financial planning, and operational risk; a lender needs to understand transition costs and risks.

findings.headline: MTFS projects £18m revenue gap in 2026-27 requiring reserve drawdown, escalating to potentially £85m by year four
findings.detail: The council's Medium Term Financial Strategy for 2026-30 shows a structural revenue funding gap of £18m in 2026-27 that must be covered by drawing earmarked reserves. The gap grows to £36m in year two and potentially £85m by year four. The financial pressure reflects over a decade of austerity combined with significant growth in social care and special education needs spending.
findings.matters: A lender must understand reserve depletion trajectories and revenue sustainability; relying on reserves to cover £18m-£85m annual deficits indicates structural financial imbalance and materially constrains borrowing capacity and financial resilience.
findings.figures: £18m deficit year 1, £36m year 2, potentially £85m year 4
findings.quote: The MTFS for 2026-30 projects a revenue gap of £18m in the first year that (subject to changes from later information such as the final Local Government Finance Settlement) will need to be balanced by the use of earmarked reserves. There is then a gap of £36m in year two potentially rising to £85m in year four.

findings.headline: Significant staffing vacancies in Strategic and Operational Property Services preventing full delivery of the asset management action plan
findings.detail: The council cannot fully resource Strategic and Operational Property Services to execute the Corporate Asset Management Plan. Despite prioritising recruitment, a 'significant number of vacancies' persist because of market buoyancy and limited supply of suitably qualified staff. This staffing gap directly constrains the council's ability to manage its assets and capital programme.
findings.matters: Staffing gaps directly limit the council's capacity to manage £521m in assets and deliver a £501m capital programme during a period of tight finances; understaffing increases risk of ineffective asset stewardship and delayed problem identification.
findings.figures: Specific vacancy numbers not disclosed; constraint described as significant
findings.quote: However, at the present time there are a significant number of vacancies across the service and whilst recruitment of additional staff is being prioritised the buoyancy of the market and the limited supply of suitably qualified people are constraining the process.

findings.headline: Capital programme project delivery slipping: only 60% of planned 2025-26 completions were delivered on schedule
findings.detail: Of 25 projects scheduled for completion during 2025-26, only 15 were delivered on time. Major school expansion projects remain incomplete: Hastings High School expansion, Birchwood School expansion (Melton Mowbray), Iveshead Secondary School extension, and phases 3–4 of Airfield Farm Business Park. Projects are cited as affected by changed economic conditions, revised service requirements and planning delays.
findings.matters: Capital programme delays indicate project management challenges and potential cost overruns; delays affect school place capacity and tie up capital that could be redeployed to other priorities.

findings.quote: Of the 25 projects due for completion during 2025–26, or with a phase due for completion in that year, 15 were completed on schedule, representing 60%. The remaining projects were primarily affected by changed economic conditions, revised service requirements and planning delays.

findings.headline: Asset management KPI performance declined sharply to 52% achieved in 2025-26 from 67% in 2024-25
findings.detail: Only 52% of the council's 25 key performance indicators across asset management were achieved, marking a 15-point drop year-on-year. The decline reflects construction cost inflation driving maintenance costs and backlogs above target levels. Three corporate landlord KPIs failed including maintenance backlog targets; six IILP portfolio indicators failed in a constrained capital growth market.
findings.matters: Declining KPI performance indicates deteriorating management of the council's £521m property portfolio during a period of acute financial stress; this signals reduced asset stewardship capability at a time of constrained resources.
findings.figures: 52% vs 67% year-on-year; 3 corporate landlord indicators failed, 6 IILP indicators failed
findings.quote: Overall, 13 of the 25 performance indicators assessed across the three categories in 2025–26, 52% were achieved, compared with 67% in 2024–25.

findings.headline: Essential maintenance liability increased by £2.7m in one year to £53.8m, with £1.8m requiring urgent remedial work within 12 months
findings.detail: The council's estimated liabilities for essential maintenance, repairs and improvements to meet health and safety and regulatory compliance increased significantly during 2025-26. The £1.8m of priority 1 work (3.3% of total) must be addressed within 12 months. This represents a growing unfunded liability within a portfolio of 710 assets.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand hidden liabilities and future capital commitments; £53.8m in deferred maintenance represents a future call on the council's cash and may signal underinvestment in asset condition during financial stress.
findings.figures: £2.7m increase, £53.8m total estimated liability, £1.8m within 12 months (priority 1)
findings.quote: The estimated future liabilities for essential maintenance, repair and improvements required to meet health and safety and regulatory compliance requirements increased by £2.7m during 2025–26 to £53.8m across the Council's property portfolio. Of this, £1.8 m, or 3.3%, falls within the most urgent priority 1 category and requires issues to be addressed within 12 months.

findings.headline: Council maintains £388m cash balance and is £63m under-borrowed, using internal funding instead of market borrowing for capital investment
findings.detail: Leicestershire holds £387.5m in short-term investments and £388m total cash balance as at 31 March 2026. The Council is £63m under-borrowed relative to its Capital Financing Requirement (CFR), internally funding this gap from cash reserves rather than raising external debt. This is cost-effective in current conditions (investment returns ~4% vs 6%+ cost of long-term borrowing) and provides headroom, but sustainability depends on disciplined capital spending and cash management.
findings.matters: Strong liquidity buffers creditors, but large cash balances tied to internal borrowing represent opportunity cost and depletion risk as capital programmes accelerate and base rates fall
findings.figures: £387.5m short-term investment portfolio, £388m cash balance, £63m under-borrowed vs CFR, portfolio averaged £439m during year (range £387m-£477m)
findings.quote: Compared with the capital financing requirement (CFR - the level of historic capital expenditure required to be funded) the Council was forecast to be £63m under borrowed as at 31 March 2026, which can be funded using internal investment balances rather than more expensive external borrowing.

findings.headline: UK gilt yields at 20+ year highs are making external borrowing expensive; council funds capital programme from internal reserves instead of market access
findings.detail: UK gilt yields have risen to their highest levels this century as at end of 2025/26 and into May 2026. These yields underpin PWLB rates and determine the cost of external borrowing. In response, the Council's capital programme (£65m requirement 2026-2030) is planned to be funded from internal balances rather than market borrowing. This pattern has been consistent since August 2010, when the Council last raised new external loans.
findings.matters: Rising gilt yields increase refinancing risk and explain 16 years without market access; the strategy is only viable while internal cash balances remain strong, and poses refinancing risk if capital spending needs accelerate beyond cash generation
findings.figures: Gilt yields at 20+ year highs, PWLB average rate on remaining debt 5.54%, £65m capital programme 2026-2030, no external borrowing since August 2010
findings.quote: Moreover, borrowing has become more expensive in 2025/26. UK gilt yields have risen materially by year end, and into May 2026 to their highest yields this century.

findings.headline: Pooled property fund losses of £0.5m realized in 2025/26 after property price falls triggered liquidation of two investment funds
findings.detail: Two of four pooled property funds (Hermes and Lothbury) that Leicestershire committed to between 2015-2019 have been liquidated following redemption requests from large investors. Liquidations occurred when property valuations had fallen due to interest rate rises in 2022-2023. In 2025/26, final redemptions resulted in the Council recognizing a £0.5m loss on capital, funded through reserves. Across the broader long-term investment portfolio (£51.9m principal), there is currently a £1.5m unrealised gain.
findings.matters: Realized losses signal real estate market exposure and reserve depletion; unrealised gains across the portfolio create downside risk if market conditions deteriorate further
findings.figures: £0.5m loss on capital realized in 2025/26, £4.7m income received over life of funds, £51.9m long-term investments held, £1.5m unrealised gain
findings.quote: Two of the funds, Hermes and Lothbury have now been liquidated... During 2025/26 the final returns of capital were received which resulted in the Council recognising a loss on capital of £0.5m

findings.headline: Treasury interest income beat budget by £4.6m (£16.6m actual vs £12m budgeted) but is flagged as unsustainable as base rates are expected to fall

Treasury advisors forecast rates stable at 3.75% through summer 2027. The Council explicitly cautions this level of return is unlikely to be sustained medium-to-long term as reserves are drawn down.
findings.matters: Lenders assessing revenue stability need to understand this one-time windfall will not recur, making underlying budget pressures more acute than headline 2025/26 figures suggest
findings.figures: £16.6m actual vs £12m budgeted interest income (£4.6m overperformance), average portfolio return 4.69%, base rate forecast 3.75% stable until summer 2027
findings.quote: The actual interest received from treasury management activities at year end was £16.6m... This overperformance is due to the BoE base rate levels being higher and for longer than forecast

findings.headline: Leicestershire reduced external debt to £130.5m (lowest in 20 years) but paid £3.5m premium upfront to refinance, sacrificing liquidity for long-term savings
findings.detail: The Council repaid £44.5m of PWLB debt in two tranches (September 2025 and March 2026), reducing total external debt from £175m to £130.5m. Early repayment required paying £3.5m in premiums upfront. Treasury advisors calculated this generates net savings of £1m pa in interest payments because the effective rate saved (7.16%) significantly exceeds forecast long-term earning rates (3.50%).
findings.matters: Debt reduction improves financial stability, but the large premiums paid and absence of market borrowing since 2010 raise questions about whether the council has tested its refinancing capability in current market conditions
findings.figures: £44.5m repaid in 2025/26, £130.5m external debt at 31/3/26 (lowest in 20+ years), £3.5m premium paid, £1m pa interest savings, 7.16% effective rate saved
findings.quote: The Council's actual level of external debt at 31st March 2026 was £130m, the lowest level for over 20 years.

Budget submissions for 2026-27 expected to show majority of schools requiring deficit licenses, with some unable to achieve balanced budgets within the 3-5 year timeframe. Internal Audit issued High Importance recommendation May 2026. Council establishing Dedicated Schools Sustainability workstream and commissioning external support to review budget submissions.
findings.matters: Widespread deficits across maintained schools that cannot be resolved within a standard planning cycle signal structural cost pressures or demand/funding misalignment that threatens service continuity
findings.figures: £3.6m net deficit as at 31/3/2026; 65 maintained schools; majority will require deficit licenses for 3-5 years

Some schools may not be able to achieve a balanced budget within this timeframe.

Efficiency Review identified £27m potential savings over MTFS, in addition to existing Strategic Change Programme savings initiatives.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Provisional Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: High Needs Block deficit surging to £99.1m in 2025-26, up 54% from £64.4m prior year
findings.detail: The deficit is rising despite TSIL programme achieving planned savings, driven by increased EHCP assessments and in-year specialist placement moves following the government's SEND White Paper. Government has announced support measures but details remain pending. DfE responsibility for funding transfers from councils from April 2028. Senior leaders continue to scrutinise high-cost placements and expand maintained specialist provision.
findings.matters: A £99m deficit in a single service area, even with prospective government support, represents a critical financial strain that impacts reserves and constrains the council's ability to invest in other priorities or absorb financial shocks
findings.figures: £99.1m deficit 2025-26 (vs £64.4m 2024-25); government funding mechanism for repayment still to be confirmed
findings.quote: the High Needs deficit is forecast to rise from £64.4m (2024/25) to £99.1m (2025/26)

findings.headline: Budget Equalisation reserve increased by £28m, suggesting anticipated future budget pressures
findings.detail: The council's Budget Equalisation reserve — used to smooth budget volatility — grew from £62.1m to £90.4m, an increase of £28.3m or 45.6%. This substantial build-up may indicate the council is deliberately setting aside more to cover expected shortfalls in future years.
findings.matters: While building reserves is prudent, a substantial increase in this equalisation fund may signal the council's own finance team expects significant budget pressures ahead, which would matter to a lender assessing forward-looking sustainability.
findings.figures: Budget Equalisation reserve increased from £62,107k to £90,447k; increase of £28,340k
findings.quote: Budget Equalisation 62,107 90,447

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit grew by £31m in a single year to £79m
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant reserve, which tracks accumulated deficits or surpluses on school funding, deteriorated from a deficit of £48.3m in April 2025 to £79.2m by March 2026. This represents a year-on-year worsening of £30.9m. The reserve is negative and growing significantly more negative.
findings.matters: A growing DSG deficit indicates systemic pressures in school funding that the council must carry forward. For lenders, a deficit of this scale and trajectory signals financial stress and reduces headroom for managing other service pressures.
findings.figures: Dedicated Schools Grant reserve moved from -£48,349k to -£79,244k; deterioration of £30,895k
findings.quote: Dedicated Schools Grant -48,349 -79,244

findings.headline: Investing in Leicestershire Programme office portfolio is under stress with £1.2m adverse variance due to voids and 'increasingly competitive office market'; expected to continue into 2026-27
findings.detail: The IiLP (council's investment property portfolio used to generate income supporting MTFS) recorded net income of £8.6m for 2025-26 in line with budget, but the directly owned property estate showed a £1.2m adverse variance. The report specifically attributes this to 'voids in an increasingly competitive office market (lower occupancy) of £0.8m'. The council states 'The tougher office rental sector is expected to continue in 2026/27.' The full-year net income return on IiLP is 3.5% when including development assets (much lower than core holdings at 5.8%). The council holds property both for income and 'capital appreciation' but is underperforming on income.
findings.matters: The IiLP is a material part of the council's MTFS assumptions. If office income continues to deteriorate and capital appreciation is uncertain in a recessionary market, the council's reserve-building assumptions may prove optimistic. The shift from income focus to capital appreciation suggests the council is expecting to take losses on operations to realise gains on exit.
findings.figures: IiLP net income £8.6m (in budget), direct property adverse variance £1.2m, office voids £0.8m, net income return 3.5% (including development assets), expected to worsen 2026-27
findings.quote: The pressure on the direct property estate in 2025/26 has been offset by favourable variances within the diversifier investments... The tougher office rental sector is expected to continue in 2026/27.

findings.headline: MTFS shows a budget gap of £84m by 2029/30; council is relying on unproven Efficiency Review savings of £27m (potential £60m by 2030/31) to close it
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Strategy covering 2026-30 shows cumulative budget gaps. The report states 'the current MTFS for 2026-30 is still extremely challenging and shows a gap of £84m by 2029/30.' The council has commissioned an Efficiency Review (Newton Consulting) that has identified £27m of savings over the MTFS period, with 'potential to stretch to almost £60m of savings by 2030/31'. These opportunities are being 'combined with the Council's existing MTFS savings plans' into a transformation programme. The council is allocating £20m upfront for implementation costs (£10m from MTFS, £8m from contingency, £2m from 2025-26 underspend).
findings.matters: A lender must assess the credibility and achievability of £27-60m of savings over the next 5 years against a backdrop of proven difficulties in delivering SEND reform, placement cost control, and demand management. The council's track record on MTFS savings delivery is not transparent from this report. Implementation costs of £20m suggest major service/structural changes ahead, which create delivery risk.
findings.figures: MTFS gap £84m by 2029/30, Efficiency Review identifies £27m savings (potential £60m by 2030/31), £20m upfront implementation allocation, £15.4m reserve drawn to balance 2026/27 budget
findings.quote: However the current MTFS for 2026-30 is still extremely challenging and shows a gap of £84m by 2029/30... The review has identified savings of £27m over the MTFS period, with the potential to stretch to almost £60m of savings by 20230/31.

findings.headline: Children's social care placement costs are driven by market failures in unregistered provision: council is paying £13,000-£17,000/week for unregulated placements when registered alternatives are unavailable
findings.detail: The Children's Social Care Placements budget overspent by £5.1m in 2025-26. The council budgeted for 5 children in unregistered/unregulated placements but the number peaked at 15 in autumn and remained elevated throughout the year. These placements cost £13,000-£17,000 per week. Additionally, the council had to place a 'small number of children in secure provision' at £35,000+ per week (historically capped at £15,000). The report notes 'there is currently a gap in the market to support these children' and many providers are 'unable to care for children due to complex needs'.
findings.matters: This is not a one-year blip but a structural market failure that will persist. The council cannot control placement costs where no registered alternatives exist. Average residential placement numbers ended at 122 vs a budget of 120, but the cost variance is driven by the 200%+ price premium on unregistered provision. A lender must understand this is a cost the council cannot easily reduce.
findings.figures: Placements budget overspend £5.1m, unregistered placements £13,000-£17,000/week (budgeted for 5, peaked at 15), secure provision £35,000+/week (vs historical £15,000), overall children's social care placement demand exceeded budget
findings.quote: Unregistered placements are used when no other option is available and are more costly than registered residential placements, with the average weekly cost of such provision ranging from between £13,000 to £17,000 over the last 12 months. The placement budget allowed funding for up to 5 children in this provision type over the financial year. However for the majority of the financial year actual numbers in this provision type have exceeded that (to a peak of 15 in the autumn).

findings.headline: General Fund reserve is now at the lower end of the approved range (4.2%) and must be actively rebuilt to absorb future MTFS gaps
findings.detail: The General Fund reserve stands at £26m, representing 4.2% of the 2026/27 revenue budget. This is within the approved policy range of 4% to 7% but explicitly 'at the lower end'. The report notes it is 'necessary to increase the General Fund to reflect increasing uncertainty and risks over the medium term' and the MTFS includes contributions of £1m per year to rebuild it. The 2026/27 budget is only balanced by using £15.4m of reserves.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion signals reduced financial resilience. A council at the lower end of its reserve policy range has limited headroom to absorb adverse variances, unexpected cost shocks, or slower savings delivery. The need for £1m annual contributions going forward suggests the council does not believe discretionary reserves can grow.
findings.figures: General Fund £26m (4.2% of 2026/27 budget), approved range 4-7%, £1m annual contribution planned, 2026/27 budget requires £15.4m reserves to balance
findings.quote: The General Fund reserve stands at £26m as at 31 March 2026, which represents 4.2% of the 2026/27 revenue budget... As this is at the lower end of the approved range, the MTFS 2026-30 includes contributions of £1m per year to increase the General Fund.

findings.headline: DSG High Needs deficit has blown to £99m and is projected to reach £400m by 2030 if demand continues on current trajectory
findings.detail: The High Needs Block deficit grew from £64.4m at March 2025 to £99.1m at March 2026. The overall net cumulative DSG deficit across all blocks stands at £79.2m. The primary driver is sustained growth in Education, Health and Care Plans: 8,983 active EHCPs by April 2026, representing a 193% increase since 2016 and a 23% increase year-on-year. The council describes the financial position as 'unsustainable' despite mitigation efforts through the Transforming SEND programme.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether reserves can sustainably absorb this deficit or whether the council's balance sheet will deteriorate faster than the MTFS assumes. At £99m, this is material to council solvency and government is only funding 90% (approx £71m), leaving £28-32m to be funded from reserves.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £79.2m (net across all blocks, up from £48.3m), High Needs Block specifically £99.1m, EHCPs up 193% since 2016, 23% YoY growth, projected deficit to £400m+ by March 2030 if demand trajectory continues
findings.quote: If future demand remained on a similar trajectory to 2025/26, the cumulative DSG deficit could increase to upwards of £400m by March 2030.

findings.headline: High Needs DSG deficit forecast to grow from £64m to over £400m by 2029/30
findings.detail: The High Needs element of Dedicated Schools Grant is running a substantial and growing deficit. It stood at £64m in deficit as at 31 March 2025, and is forecast to increase to more than £400m by the end of 2029/30. The council is holding this as a Budget Equalisation and Transformation earmarked reserve.
findings.matters: A £400m+ escalating liability on the council's balance sheet represents a major structural funding gap in schools finance that will require sustained central support or service changes, materially affecting the council's financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £64m deficit at 31 March 2025; forecast to increase to more than £400m by end of 2029/30
findings.quote: the increasing pressures on the High Needs element of the DSG which was in deficit by £64m as at 31 March 2025 and is forecast to increase to more than £400m by the end of 2029/30.

findings.headline: General Fund balance at £30m (4.2%) is at the lower end of the 4-7% target range, reflecting tighter financial pressures
findings.detail: The council sets a target for General Fund balance of 4-7% of net expenditure. The forecast balance by the end of the Medium Term Financial Strategy is £30m, which represents 4.2% - explicitly described as being at the lower end of the acceptable range and as reflecting the council's tighter financial pressures.
findings.matters: A minimum-level reserve provides little buffer against unexpected financial shocks, increasing financial risk and leaving the council vulnerable to any further funding deterioration.
findings.figures: £30m (4.2%) forecast balance; target range 4-7% of net expenditure
findings.quote: The forecast balance of £ 30m (4.2%), by the end of the MTFS is at the lower end of that range reflecting the tighter financial pressures of the Council.

findings.headline: Operational borrowing boundary rising by £61m from 2026/27 to 2029/30, signalling significant increase in debt stock
findings.detail: The council is approving an operational boundary for borrowing of £194m in 2026/27, rising to £255m in 2029/30 (increase of £61m). The authorised limit rises from £204m to £265m. The MTFS also raises the prudential borrowing limits significantly in outer years, reaching £235m and £265m in the authorised limit by 2029/30.
findings.matters: A lender must understand that the council expects to increase its debt stock substantially, and should assess debt service capacity and the timing and drivers of this borrowing.
findings.figures: Operational boundary borrowing: 2026/27 £194m, 2027/28 £200m, 2028/29 £225m, 2029/30 £255m; Authorised limit rising from £204m to £265m
findings.quote: That the following borrowing limits be approved for the period 2026/27 to 2029/30: ... Operational boundary for external debt i) Borrowing 194 200 225 255

findings.headline: Capital programme shortfall of £75m addressed with only £10m from reserves, driving rising borrowing requirement
findings.detail: The four-year capital programme totals £501m but the council faces a £75m capital shortfall. The response is to transfer £10m from the budget equalisation reserve to the capital financing reserve. This addresses only one-seventh of the shortfall, meaning prudential borrowing will need to increase significantly. The operational borrowing boundary rises from £194m in 2026/27 to £255m by 2029/30.
findings.matters: Unmet capital funding typically drives increases in prudential borrowing, which affects debt service costs and constrains financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £75m capital shortfall; £501m capital programme; £10m reserve redirection; borrowing boundary rising from £194m to £255m
findings.quote: £10m transferred to the capital financing reserve to reduce the capital shortfall of £75m and reduce the need for prudential borrowing in later years of the MTFS

findings.headline: 2027/28 budget gap of £34.2m depends on savings plans that are still under development
findings.detail: Following the final settlement, the 2027/28 budget gap stands at £34.2m. The council's response is to ask Chief Officers to develop transformation proposals to close the gap in all four years of the MTFS. The MTFS explicitly includes 'savings under development' (Appendix D) rather than committed savings, meaning the specific proposals to achieve these reductions have not yet been finalised or approved.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know how budget gaps will be closed. Savings described as 'under development' rather than committed create uncertainty about feasibility and delivery risk.
findings.figures: £34.2m budget gap in 2027/28; four-year MTFS includes undefined 'savings under development'
findings.quote: Each Chief Officer, in consultation with the Director of Corporate Resources and following consultation with the relevant Cabinet Lead Member(s), undertake preparatory work as considered appropriate to develop proposals and associated investment required to reduce the financial gap in all four years of the MTFS

findings.headline: Council redirecting £35m of High Needs deficit reserves to LGR, capital financing and efficiency programmes, leaving limited contingency for unconfirmed DSG support
findings.detail: Leicestershire held £65m in budget equalisation reserves against future High Needs deficits. With government grant covering £80m of the March 2026 deficit, the council is reallocating £35m: £10m for Local Government Reorganisation costs, £10m to reduce capital financing shortfall, £10m for Efficiency Review implementation, and £2.5m to the Service Investment Fund. Only £2.5m is retained in the budget equalisation reserve. This leaves minimal cover if Phase 2 DSG support is lower than assumed.
findings.matters: The council is spending contingency reserves on structural change programmes rather than maintaining buffer for DSG deficits that remain unresolved and unconfirmed.
findings.figures: £65m reserve at 31 March 2026; £35m redirected; £2.5m retained; £80m government grant assumption
findings.quote: A total of £35m is therefore proposed to be redirected towards other priorities of the Council and to support the MTFS in the longer term

findings.headline: Government support for Dedicated Schools Grant deficits from 2026/27 onwards is not yet confirmed and stated to be 'not unlimited'
findings.detail: The council has a £110m High Needs Block deficit forecast at March 2026. Government will cover up to 90% of this deficit (estimated £80m) but only after DfE approval of a SEND reform plan. For deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28, government has not yet confirmed support levels, and the DfE will scrutinise accounts for 'ineligible spend' which will be deducted from the grant calculation. The council is setting aside only 50% of forecast future deficits 'until the position becomes clearer'.
findings.matters: The council's budget assumes government grant support that is contingent, unconfirmed, and potentially subject to audit challenge, creating material cash flow risk.
findings.figures: £110m High Needs Block deficit; estimated £80m government grant for March 2026; remaining £30m council-funded; Phase 2 support to be confirmed by 31 March 2028
findings.quote: the Government will confirm the detail on further support for deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28 before the end of the statutory override (31 March 2028), stating 'we will continue to take an appropriate and proportionate approach, although it will not be unlimited'

findings.headline: Invest-to-save schemes approved below 7% return threshold when there is an 'overriding policy objective', meaning non-financial rationale drives capital allocation.
findings.detail: The strategy requires invest-to-save schemes to demonstrate 7% return. But the council reserves the right to approve lower-return schemes: 'Only projects that show a positive return using these rates will be considered for inclusion in the capital programme, unless there is an overriding policy objective that justifies a lower rate with the Director of Corporate Resources agreement.' This means capital is being committed on grounds other than financial return.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that capital investments will deliver promised returns. Non-financial approval criteria increase the risk that investments underperform and savings do not materialise.
findings.figures: 7% minimum return threshold; overridable by Director of Corporate Resources
findings.quote: unless there is an overriding policy objective that justifies a lower rate with the Director of Corporate Resources agreement

findings.headline: Capital receipts target of £23m over four years depends on planning permissions being granted, introducing timing uncertainty and downside risk.
findings.detail: Strategic Property Services targets £23m in capital receipts across 2026-30. However, the council acknowledges: 'The estimates include potential land sales that are subject to planning permission. In these cases the value of the site is significantly increased when planning permission is approved. However, this also comes with a significant amount of uncertainty and potential for delays.'
findings.matters: A material discretionary funding source depends on external approval and carries timing risk. Planning delays or lower valuations would force alternative funding or scheme deferrals.
findings.figures: £23.1m capital receipts target (£3.1m in 2026/27, peaking at £10.2m in 2027/28)
findings.quote: However, this also comes with a significant amount of uncertainty and potential for delays.

findings.headline: Revenue budget already unable to fund capital: zero ongoing revenue contributions expected, reliance only on one-off reserves and underspends.
findings.detail: The capital programme includes £83m from one-off funding (prior-year underspends, released reserves). The council states plainly: 'Given the Councils financial situation there have been no on-going revenue contributions to the capital programme for a number of years.' This means the revenue budget is too tight to contribute to capital investment, a sign of underlying budget stress.
findings.matters: This signals the revenue budget is constrained and cannot sustain capital investment. Future capital programmes will depend on either unsustainable reserve drawdown or further borrowing.
findings.figures: £83m one-off revenue funding; £0m ongoing revenue contribution
findings.quote: Given the Councils financial situation there have been no on-going revenue contributions to the capital programme for a number of years.

findings.headline: Section 106 forward funding: £5m of previously forward-funded infrastructure repayment at risk, contingent on developer contributions that may take many years to materialise.
findings.detail: The council previously forward-funded £20m in infrastructure. Of this, £9.5m has been repaid, £5.5m is estimated to repay by 2030, but £5m repayment is pushed after 2030. The council states the repayment is essential for sustainability: 'The Council's medium and longer term financial strategies are only sustainable if this funding is recovered.' The risk is explicit: 'Risks could be further compounded in the event of an economic slowdown, which could delay the housing development required before section 106 contributions are to be paid.'
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that future revenue will be sufficient to absorb delayed developer contributions. If housing development stalls, repayment extends further, worsening the council's cash position.
findings.figures: £20m originally forward-funded; £5m repayment after 2030; potential risk from economic slowdown and construction inflation
findings.quote: The Council's medium and longer term financial strategies are only sustainable if this funding is recovered.

findings.headline: £75 million prudential borrowing required at £6m per annum for 40 years, explicitly framed as a 'significant commitment' against wider financial pressures.
findings.detail: The capital programme totals £501m but external funding covers only £320m. Of the £181m balance needed, £75m must come from prudential borrowing to fund schools and highway infrastructure. The council explicitly acknowledges this commitment is difficult: 'This is a significant commitment to the Council given its wider financial pressures.' Annual financing costs (interest and MRP) rise from £12m in 2026/27 to £13.4m by 2029/30.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether the council can afford new debt alongside existing pressures. This language signals the council is already strained and this borrowing is straining it further.
findings.figures: £75m prudential borrowing; £6m per annum revenue cost over 40 years; £501m total capital programme; £12m-£13.4m annual financing costs
findings.quote: This is a significant commitment to the Council given its wider financial pressures.

findings.headline: Council Tax increase capped at 2.99%, indicating limited flexibility on this lever
findings.detail: The Cabinet recommends a 2.99% Council Tax increase. This is at the maximum available without triggering a referendum (up to 2% general increase plus 3% social care precept). Using the full allowance suggests limited room for further Council Tax rises in future years.
findings.matters: Exhausting the Council Tax precept lever signals that future budget gaps cannot be closed via Council Tax rises; they must be addressed through savings, borrowing, or reserves.
findings.figures: 2.99% Council Tax increase 2026/27
findings.quote: The Cabinet at its meeting recommended a Council Tax increase of 2.99%

findings.headline: Leicester and Leicestershire Business Rate Pool revoked for 2026/27, removing income pooling arrangement
findings.detail: The council notes the revocation of its business rate pool partnership with Leicester. Business rate pooling provides income smoothing by allowing councils to share volatility in business rate revenues; revocation removes this buffer.
findings.matters: Loss of a pooling arrangement represents both lost income (amount unquantified here) and reduced buffer against business rate volatility; a new headwind in a year already facing gaps in years 2-4.
findings.figures: Business rate pool revoked (quantum of income loss not stated)
findings.quote: The Leicester and Leicestershire Business Rate Pool has been revoked for 2026/27

findings.headline: Authorised borrowing limit rises from £204m to £265m (36% increase over the MTFS period)
findings.detail: The Council is approving borrowing limits that increase from £204m in 2026/27 to £265m in 2029/30. Operational boundaries show the same steep trajectory (£194m to £255m). The increase appears to front-load in later years (£235m by 2028/29), suggesting anticipated capital or revenue funding needs.
findings.matters: Accelerating debt limits combined with unresolved revenue deficits raises questions about whether borrowing is funding capital investment or bridging revenue gaps.
findings.quote: Authorised limit for external debt: Borrowing £204m (2026/27) ... £265m (2029/30)

findings.headline: Council has unresolved financial gaps across 2027/28 to 2029/30 with savings still under development
findings.detail: The Cabinet motion directs officers to 'undertake preparatory work...to develop proposals and associated investment required to reduce the financial gap in all four years of the MTFS'. This means the approved budget does not include confirmed savings proposals for years 2-4, only 'savings under development' listed in Appendix D.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that a council can close structural deficits; unresolved gaps into year 4 suggest budget pressures may require either service cuts, further borrowing, or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £613.4m net revenue budget 2026/27; gaps in years 2027/28, 2028/29, 2029/30 (quantum not disclosed in this extract)
findings.quote: To develop proposals and associated investment required to reduce the financial gap in all four years of the MTFS

findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision methodology changed to annuity basis with 2% annual increases from 2025/26
findings.detail: Council moved from fixed 40-year repayment period (since 2019/20) to annuity-basis calculation with inflation-linked increases at 2% per year, approved February 2025 and applied from 2025/26. This recent change affects forward budget projections and the timing of capital repayment.
findings.matters: Recent methodology change affects the accuracy of council's medium-term financial projections; the shift to inflation-linked increases means rising annual MRP charges (as shown in forecasts), which cumulative impact on revenue budget over the capital programme lifespan.
findings.figures: 2% annuity inflation rate; total MRP charge structure changed February 2025
findings.quote: The revised approach was approved by the Council in February 2025 and is being applied from 2025/26.

findings.headline: £260m investment portfolio subject to annual compliance review under new PWLB restrictions on borrowing for return
findings.detail: Council holds £260m in investments (at historic cost) primarily generating financial return, currently yielding ~£9m annually. Recent HM Treasury guidance (2023) restricts PWLB access if any capital schemes are primarily for return. Where a council needs external or internal borrowing (as Leicestershire forecasts), it must annually review whether to exit return-seeking investments, creating ongoing policy uncertainty.
findings.matters: The mandatory annual exit review introduces regulatory risk and potential constraint on the council's capital programme; the large portfolio (£260m) is material to council finances and relies on sustained income generation.
findings.figures: £260m existing holdings, £9m annual income excluding capital growth, £43m additional IiLP investment proposed
findings.quote: However, where the Council has an expected need to borrow (internally or externally), as does the County Council for the wider capital programme, the Code requires an annual review of options to exit inves tments held primarily for return.

findings.headline: Council funding new borrowing from internal cash balances, not external PWLB
findings.detail: The capital financing strategy assumes new borrowing required for the capital programme will be met from internal cash balances rather than public market borrowing. This approach relies on reserve adequacy and has implications for the council's liquidity position and cash flow flexibility.
findings.matters: Reliance on internal cash reserves for borrowing rather than external markets raises questions about reserve adequacy to support capital spending and operational requirements, particularly as borrowing need grows to £14m+ per year.
findings.figures: Not specified in document
findings.quote: This estimate assumes the required new borrowing is from internal cash balances.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs forecast to rise from £12.4m in 2026/27 to £14m in 2029/30 due to new borrowing requirement
findings.detail: The council forecasts capital financing costs—comprising Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) on an annuity basis plus external debt interest—will increase by £1.6m over four years. This rise is explicitly attributed to the requirement for new borrowing within the wider capital programme, representing material growth in the revenue budget commitment to debt service.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the trajectory of the council's debt service obligations and their impact on revenue budget; finance directors must plan sustained revenue provision for rising capital financing costs.
findings.quote: Overall capital financing costs , MRP (annuity basis)  and external debt interest, are forecast to be £12.4m in 2026/27 and to then rise to £14m in 2029/30 as a result of the requirement for new borrowing.

findings.headline: Journal authorization controls: no approval required for entries under £20,000; senior staff approved by juniors
findings.detail: The audit noted that journals posted below £20,000 do not require authorization. Additionally, instances were identified where journals posted by senior team members were approved by junior staff, contrary to best practice which would require approval by a more senior individual to ensure appropriate oversight.
findings.matters: Material misstatement risk; lack of proper authorization hierarchy and high authorization thresholds increase potential for unauthorized or erroneous transactions to be recorded without detection.

findings.headline: Property valuation controls weak: no formal terms of engagement with valuer
findings.detail: The Council's valuation of County Hall was found to be understated by £1.019m. The audit also identified that no formal Terms of Engagement documents have been received from the valuer, only outline instructions. The auditors recommend the Council establish specific Terms of Engagement for each valuation instruction to ensure accountability and clarity of scope.
findings.matters: Property assets represent the Council's largest balance sheet item; weak valuation governance and documentation creates risk of material misstatement and signals broader control environment gaps.
findings.figures: £1.019m understatement identified

It is our view that for each instruction, the Council should ensure it has specific Terms of Engagement document to help establish accountability, ensure clarity on the scope and objectives, and provide an audit trail.

findings.detail: The auditors identified two material misstatements that were not adjusted: the pension liability was understated by £1.671m and land and buildings (specifically County Hall) were understated by £1.019m. The Council has chosen not to adjust these on materiality grounds, requiring specific representations in the Letter of Representation.
findings.matters: Unadjusted misstatements indicate either weak internal controls or a deliberate decision to remain beneath materiality thresholds; lenders need to understand the gap between stated and economic position.

findings.quote: We have identified two unadjusted misstatements to the Council's financial statements, one relating to the valuation of the Council's net pension liability, an understatement of £1.671m and one relating to the valuation of the Council's land and buildings, an understatement of £1.019m.

Although the Government has extended the Statutory Override to March 2028, the Council still needs to fund the in-year overspending, and a key recommendation has been made.
findings.matters: A cumulative deficit forecast to more than double in three years without additional government support poses a material threat to financial sustainability and may force significant service reductions or reserves drawdown.
